title: HCV-Associated Extrahepatic Malignancies: The Infection – Autoimmunity - Cancer Paradigm
content: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is a well-established cause of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and potentially associated with different extrahepatic immune-mediated, lymphoproliferative, and neoplastic disorders. The clinical spectrum linking hepatic disease, autoimmunity, lymphoproliferation, and cancer has been conceptualized as the "HCV syndrome." This narrative review is an updated overview of the historical evolution, epidemiological evidence, pathogenic mechanisms, and therapeutic implications of HCV-associated extrahepatic malignancies. The major studies, including the historical identification of HCV as hepatotropic and lymphotropic virus, epidemiology of HCV-associated malignancies, direct/indirect oncogenic mechanisms, and effects of direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapies were reported. HCV-associated oncogenesis represents a multifactorial and multistep process involving both indirect mechanisms—persistent antigenic stimulation, chronic inflammation, immune-system activation, and dysregulation—and potential direct effects of viral proteins. HCV lymphotropism provides a major biological basis for persistent B-cell oligo-/monoclonal expansion, and progression towards B-NHL. Mixed cryoglobulinemia syndrome represents a relevant clinico-biological crossroads between autoimmunity, B-cell lymphoproliferation, and lymphoma. Epidemiological evidence suggests possible associations with selected extrahepatic solid and hematological malignancies, although causal inference remains heterogeneous and substantially weaker. Viral eradication with Direct Acting Antivirals (DAAs) provided important indirect evidence supporting the HCV role on selected lymphoproliferative disorders, while persistence of some complications after sustained virological response suggests that irreversible biological alterations may develop during chronic infection. The spectrum of HCV-associated disorders can be regarded as a dynamic "infection–autoimmunity–cancer" paradigm. Among extrahepatic malignancies, B-NHL remains the most convincing example of HCV-associated oncogenesis, whereas the role of HCV in other neoplasms requires further clarification.
